title: Energy security depends on if we electrify, and how we do it
where: The Editorial Page, page 8 (Neha Dhingra, CLASP)
syllabus: GS3 › Energy infrastructure; Conservation; Industrial policy (MSMEs) · GS2 › Energy security and foreign policy; Statutory bodies (BEE, BIS) · GS1 › Effects of globalisation on Indian society · GS4 › Innovation in public service
summary: After the Hormuz disruption hit India's LPG supply, the writer argues that electrifying industrial heat (heat pumps) and kitchens (induction) cuts import exposure, if standards and domestic supply come first.
ideas: A far-off war reached Indian kitchens: when Hormuz shipping stalled in March, families queued for cooking gas; the writer notes India imports about 60% of its LPG, nearly 90% of it via the strait.
India's LPG dependence on one chokepoint shows how a distant conflict becomes a domestic crisis within weeks.

Electrification is a security strategy: in NITI Aayog's net-zero scenario, electricity's share of final energy rises from 21% to 60% by 2070 and the fuel import bill falls from about 4% of GDP to 0.2%.
Electrification turns India's clean power base into energy security by replacing imported fuel with domestic electricity.

Industrial heat is the lowest-hanging fruit: factories burn coal, oil and gas on site for much of their energy; electrifying it cuts imports, decarbonises industry and helps exporters meet the EU's CBAM.
Electrifying industrial heat cuts fuel imports, decarbonises industry and protects exports from carbon border taxes.

How we electrify matters: a heat pump, an air conditioner in reverse, gives 2.5 to 4 units of heat per unit of electricity against at most one from an electric boiler; much MSME heat is below 250°C, within its range.
Heat pumps meet low-temperature industrial heat with a fraction of the electricity, sparing the grid new capacity.

Cost, confidence and supply hold the market back: high upfront cost, efficiency claims tested under foreign standards, and dependence on Chinese imports; Indian standards, BIS certification and a star label should come before demand surges.
GS3 · Industrial policy / GS2 · Regulatory bodies
Standards and labels before a demand surge, plus domestic manufacturing, keep electrification from importing new dependencies.

trend.t: Energy questions moved from renewable targets and sources (2013, 2015, 2016, 2022) to energy security as a strategic question, in GS2 foreign policy (2017, 2025) and GS3 challenges (2026). The newest asks how clean technology can give energy independence by 2047 (2025).
trend.watch: Energy security came in 2025 and 2026 in both papers, and the angle is shifting from adding supply to cutting dependence. Prepare electrification, efficiency and supply-chain risk together; see also the 31 October E100 card.

practice.q: "Electrification is India's most practical route to energy security." Examine with reference to industry and households.

answer.t: When shipping through Hormuz stalled in March, LPG queues formed and induction cooktops sold out, showing how a distant conflict reaches Indian kitchens.

answer.t: Electrification is the most practical path to energy security, provided India builds standards and factories before demand surges, so it does not swap a fuel dependence for an equipment one.
